platforms.title: That Lump Might Be a Cyst, Not a Lipoma
platforms.meta_description: Feeling a lump under your skin? How the AAD tells a lipoma apart from an epidermoid cyst, by texture, the central punctum, and infection risk.
platforms.body_html:
Feeling a soft lump under your skin and wondering what it is? The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) explains that lipomas and epidermoid cysts form in completely different tissue. Both are usually benign, but mixing them up and trying to squeeze or pop one at home can end up causing an infection instead of solving anything.

Why the same kind of lump has different causes

A lipoma is a benign tumor that grows in the layer of fat under the skin. It feels soft and doughy, and slides freely under your fingers when pressed. It grows slowly and is usually painless.

An epidermoid cyst comes from an entirely different tissue. It's marked by a blocked pore or oil gland that traps keratin in a sac under the skin. It feels firmer than a lipoma, often shows a small central punctum — a tiny visible pore — and is more firmly attached to the skin itself, so it doesn't move as freely when pressed.

How to tell them apart, and what to check

First, whether the lump slides freely when pressed, or feels firmly fixed in place. The AAD notes that a lipoma glides smoothly under the skin, while an epidermoid cyst is attached to the skin itself and barely moves.

Second, whether a small central dot or opening is visible. An epidermoid cyst often shows a tiny pore where the follicle got blocked. A lipoma has no such punctum at all.

What's most worth being careful about is not trying to squeeze or pop an epidermoid cyst at home. It can suddenly become red, painful, and swollen when inflamed, and forcing it open can push the contents deeper under the skin, worsening an infection or making it more likely to come back. Lipomas rarely get inflamed and usually stay stable exactly as they are.

When it's hard to tell which one is going on, it helps to check how firm the lump feels, whether there's a central punctum, and whether it's suddenly grown larger or become painful. Either type can be removed with a simple procedure at a dermatologist if it bothers you, but rapid growth, new firmness, or pain deserves a proper evaluation rather than assuming it's nothing.

Where the lump shows up offers another clue. Lipomas tend to appear on the trunk, neck, shoulders, and arms, and some people develop several of them over the years as a family trait. Epidermoid cysts show up wherever hair follicles are dense, especially the face, neck, back, and scalp, since a blocked follicle is what starts the whole process.

It's also worth knowing that a lump that keeps growing quickly, feels unusually hard, or is tender to the touch without any obvious inflammation deserves prompt medical attention, since those features are less typical of either a simple lipoma or a simple cyst and are worth ruling out other causes for.

Does the lump you're feeling slide around freely, or does it have a central dot and feel firmly attached?
